title: Fingerprints are the new cookies
author: royfish
relevanceReason: 命中 2 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: From now on I’ll call you:

Try refreshing the page. Clear the cookies. Connect to a VPN. You’re still the …. Now open it on your phone or some other device and your nickname will be different and just as consistent. Is it different in incognito? Good. But it’s always the same? Bad news. Imagine this: Most websites you visit get paid to show ads and indirectly run my script that lets me know you’re the …. I can use it to decide what ads you’ll see. But more importantly, if you’ve made an account on that website, I can offer to buy your data - whatever they can share under their privacy policy: your name, activity, conversations with AI… Pretty soon I’d know more about you than your friends do - perhaps more than you know yourself. “So what?” - you say.
“I have nothing to hide. And I prefer my ads to be relevant… sometimes they show me exactly what I need! And the data is anonymised anyway…”

See, the thing is, it’s not about you at all. It’s not really about the ads anymore either. Nobody cares about you. And if the police or your government happen to care, I’ll gladly take their money too. I look at all this data and I don’t see people. I see patterns. Patterns emerging out of patterns. A living, digital fractal state of the economy, society and human psyche. The crystal ball of the 21st century and it’s made of silicon! That’s the product. And to the highest bidder it goes! What does that make you then? A gear? An ox? A volunteer?

comments.author: alkonaut
comments.textRawHtml:
I still don't understand why the highest entropy APIs aren't gated behind browser consent.

A news site doesn't need to do audio processing on my machine and read back the buffer? It doesn't need to use webgl to render triangles to an offscreen buffer?

Broad geographical targeting shouldn't be an issue. In fact, it's so easy that I think we should invent an ad-targeting API people can opt in to. If I could tell advertisers my geographic location, gender, age cohort, languages, and 3 interests, I'd not feel that's an invasion of privacy when they use that to deliver ads. I'd just get lawnmower ads instead of shampoo ads and that's fine.

The problem is, they don't want to use that kind of targeting. They want to target me with ads for a travel destination that my coworker mentioned in a Messenger message to another coworker five minutes ago. But we should just not accept that.

children.author: rickdeckard
children.textRawHtml:
> "I still don't understand why the highest entropy APIs aren't gated behind browser consent"

Because it's known that interrupting the user-intent with a unrelated consent-popup doesn't help.

Older people may remember that this was the approach of Java J2ME, where you couldn't provide a fluent user-experience as the user first had to answer huge popups about individual API-permissions with "Always Allow", "Allow now" etc.

children.author: alkonaut
children.textRawHtml:
So long as it's once per API and site, it seems it doesn't need to be too bad?

If it's a site I trust, and I think it genuinely needs audio, I give it audio. If someone doesn't understand and just does allow all, they never see it again either (and their ads are suspiciously well targeted).

We already have these consent popups for camera and microphone. Reading back bytes from an audio buffer seems like such a rare thing to do that it hopefully just stops happening.

children.author: routerl
children.textRawHtml:
It's less rare than you'd hope. Disclosure: I do developer relations at Friendly Captcha, and our widget is one of the scripts that uses generated offline audio (but with no microphone recording) and reads the buffer back on sites that otherwise have no use for audio.

We do this to check whether the browser is what it claims to be, not to track who you are. Similarly, font rendering, floating-point math results, WebGL renderer strings, and whether built-in functions are patched is all much harder to fake. These considerations determine how hard the proof-of-work puzzle should be, and site owners can see it as a risk score. We don't do cookies or browser storage, IPs aren't stored, and nothing gets used to recognize you on another site or on a later visit. The biggest players in automated traffic prevention can't (and usually don't) say this much, because of conflicts of interest between automated bot detection and their other products (e.g. ad sales and IP-profiling).

Your example is really fair though. I chatted with our engineers, prompted by this thread, and we found nothing in our detection that currently uses the audio hashes we collect, so we've started talking about removing the collection.

children.author: qurren
children.textRawHtml:
Also, people not in tech do not generally understand the implication of consent popups.

For example, on multiple instances, my spouse declined "location permissions" an app designed to work with a piece of Bluetooth-connected hardware, and would blame the hardware as being crappy.

"This smart lock app doesn't work."

"You need to enable this permission."

"Why do I need to give the smart lock app location permissions?"

It's not obvious to people that "Bluetooth can be used sneakily by big-enough companies as a makeshift GPS" even if the app needing Bluetooth access doesn't actually need a GPS location.

children.author: Panzerschrek
children.textRawHtml:
> A news site doesn't need to do audio processing on my machine and read back the buffer? It doesn't need to use webgl to render triangles to an offscreen buffer?

We should go further. A web-site with mostly static content should not use user-side scripting (Javascript) at all, it's unnecessary for it. It should be required only in rare cases where a site is basically an application and require manually turning it on each time such application is opened.

children.author: alkonaut
children.textRawHtml: I think that ship sailed and I'm pragmatic enough to accept it. The web is an application platform, not a web of hypertext content. That's not going to change, and I've given up on the idea to even try to "go back" there. If it worked, you'd just have half of websites be "sites" that work without JS, and half would be "apps" which would require switching on JS? The whole reaosn the web took off as it has is because we removed the distinction between "web app" and "web site". There's no putting that genie back in the bottle.

children.author: jcgl
children.textRawHtml:
Sure, for the most static of static sites. But without JavaScript you can’t even do basic things client-side, such as having some variable-length list of fields in a form. Or customized field validation.

If such client-side behavior counts as “basically an application,” then “applications” is a larger set than seems useful.

children.author: TheFlyingFish
children.textRawHtml:
Theme switchers! My favorite example of why "document-only" sites might need JS. Sure, you can use @media prefers-color-scheme for defaults, and you can do checkbox/radio shenanigans to make it switchable, but there's no way to persist that preference on a static site without JS.

If you don't care about your site being static then you can track it server side, but that has big implications for his you can just your site. Sticking a little flag in localStorage really is the best solution, if you can get past ideological purity.
